Executive Summary

Dengue remains a significant and recurring public health concern across the Asia Pacific region, with increasing risks driven by climate change, urbanisation, population mobility, and environmental factors. National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (National Societies), supported by the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), play an important role in community-based preparedness, early action, prevention, and response to dengue outbreaks. In response to operational recommendations and lessons learned from dengue operations across Asia and the Americas, the IFRC Asia Pacific Regional Office (APRO) is initiating the development of a practical operational guideline for dengue preparedness and response.

The overall objective of this guideline is to strengthen health resilience in the Asia Pacific region through improved prevention, preparedness, early action, and response to dengue outbreaks. Specifically, the guideline aims to support National Societies with concise and field-oriented operational guidance that reflects local contexts, operational realities, and community-based approaches. The guideline will align with IFRC Health and Care strategies and integrate cross-cutting considerations including Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE), Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI), Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA), and Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL).

This guideline was developed through some qualitative methods consisting of country prioritisation mapping, desk review, remote and country visit data collection, along with consultation and validation processes. Desk review activities studied IFRC and National Society operational documents, global and regional guidance, national contingency plans, and technical references from World Health Organization (WHO) and other relevant partners. Primary data collection was conducted through in-depth interviews and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) involving IFRC Country Delegations/Country Cluster Delegations (CDs/CCDs), National Societies, community volunteers, and external partners. Selected country visits (to two or three countries) and remote consultations will capture practical experiences, operational challenges, lessons learned, and good practices from dengue preparedness and response operations.

This guideline provides practical operational guidance for National Societies covering prevention strategies, risk assessment and early warning triggers, preparedness and early action measures, outbreak response and coordination mechanisms, and integration of cross-cutting sectors. The guideline also includes practical tools such as checklists, implementation tips, decision trees, suggested indicators, and sample monitoring and reporting tools to support rapid deployment and evidence-based decision-making during dengue operations.

Lastly, the operational guideline is expected to strengthen National Societies’ capacity to plan, coordinate, and implement timely and effective dengue operations at community, branch or sub-national, and national levels across the Asia Pacific region.

Glossary

Anticipatory actionActions taken before a forecasted hazard or anticipated outbreak occurs, based on forecasts, early warnings, or predefined triggers, to prevent or reduce potential impacts and protect at-risk communities.
DengueA viral infection transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.
Multi-hazard responseAn approach that considers and addresses risks and needs associated with multiple hazards, which may occur simultaneously or consecutively.
Outbreak responseCoordinated actions to control disease transmission, reduce illness and deaths, and address the impacts of a disease outbreak.
PreparednessKnowledge, capacities, plans, and resources developed in advance to enable effective anticipation of, response to, and recovery from potential disasters or emergencies.
PreventionActions taken to eliminate or reduce the likelihood of hazards causing emergencies and to minimise associated risks and impacts.
Source reductioThe removal, modification, or management of mosquito breeding sites to prevent mosquito reproduction.
SurveillanceThe systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and use of health data to inform public health action.
Vector controlMeasures to reduce or eliminate disease-carrying vectors, such as mosquitoes, and prevent disease transmission.

Chapter 1. Epidemiology

1.1 Virus Transmission

Key points
  • Dengue is a mosquito borne viral disease caused by the dengue virus (DENV), which transmitted to humans through the bite of infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitos.
  • By now, dengue has four serotypes that infect human bodies namely DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4.

Dengue is a mosquito borne viral disease caused by the dengue virus (DENV), which transmitted to humans through the bite of infected female Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitos. The mosquitoes usually bite during the daytime (peak biting periods are early in the morning and in the evening at dusk).[1]

By now, dengue has four serotypes that infect human bodies namely DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Each serotypes cause different symptoms and severity which clinical spectrum from asymptomatic infected or with mild fever to moderate dengue fever (DF), dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) that can cause fatal result to death. The most common symptoms are high fever, headache, body aches, nausea, and rash. But not all infected people show symptoms. Infected people with mild effects can get better in one to two weeks with no special treatment. However, patients with severe cases should be hospitalised to recover. To pregnant women, dengue can cause pre-term birth, low birthweight and foetal distress to the babies. [2-5] Dengue could also be transmitted through organ transplants or blood transfusions from infected donors.[1]

1.2 Case Rate

Key points
  • According to WHO, 100-400 million incidences occurred annually around the world, that the dengue is currently endemic in more than 100 countries with many Asian countries are listed in the…
  • The dengue cases have grown dramatically globally in recent decades, with the number of cases reported to WHO increasing from 505,430 cases in 2000 to 14.6 million in 2024.

According to WHO, 100-400 million incidences occurred annually around the world, that the dengue is currently endemic in more than 100 countries with many Asian countries are listed in the highest risk rank.[4, 5]

The dengue cases have grown dramatically globally in recent decades, with the number of cases reported to WHO increasing from 505,430 cases in 2000 to 14.6 million in 2024. Dengue disease remains a recurring and escalating public health risk across the region, driven by climate change, urbanisation, and population mobility that is also associated with socioeconomic status and population knowledge. This disease is commonly found in tropical and sub-tropical climate worldwide, that make dengue also classified as one of 17 Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTD). Moreover, dengue is mostly found in urban and semi-urban population settings. Dengue vaccines have been available in some countries, yet the effectiveness is still under evaluation.[3, 5, 7-9] Case rates will vary from one outbreak to another. During epidemics of dengue fever, attack rates among susceptible populations are often 40–50 per cent but may reach 80–90 per cent.[1]

1.3 Environmental and Social Factors

Key points
  • Dengue transmission may occur through multiple social and environmental factors: population density, human mobility, access to reliable water source, water storage practices, etc.

Dengue transmission may occur through multiple social and environmental factors: population density, human mobility, access to reliable water source, water storage practices, etc. Therefore, whether the spread or prevention of diseases within population depends on community knowledge, attitudes and practices towards dengue.[4]

1.3.1 Environmental and Climatic Conditions

Key points
  • Climate change leads to increasing temperatures, high rainfall and humidity, giving a perfect condition for mosquitoes breeding sites, which increases the risk of mosquitoes borne diseases…
  • When the rainy season begins, the mosquito eggs that hibernate during the dry season will soon hatch.
  • The risk becomes worse when environment and climatic changes also lead to hazardous event, such as extreme weather, heavy rainfall, and flooding.

Climate change leads to increasing temperatures, high rainfall and humidity, giving a perfect condition for mosquitoes breeding sites, which increases the risk of mosquitoes borne diseases transmission like dengue. With temperatures ranging from 18° C - 35° C, humidity ranging from 60-80 per cent, and rainfall in the range of 200-800 mm are suitable for mosquito life and transmission of the dengue virus to humans. Increased dengue fever risk is at the onset of rainfall, lasting for at least three months.[3, 5, 6]

When the rainy season begins, the mosquito eggs that hibernate during the dry season will soon hatch. In relation to this hatching and the growth to adulthood, the pattern of dengue cases generally followed the rainfall around of two months. However, the interaction between the dengue virus, the host and the environment is dynamic. Vectors can adapt to new environments and climates. Consequently, dengue risks may change and shift with climate change in combination with increased urbanisation and population movement. It may cause the increasing of dengue cases also occur in suburban or rural areas, either lower or higher land area which are not in the same density as urban areas.[3, 5]

The risk becomes worse when environment and climatic changes also lead to hazardous event, such as extreme weather, heavy rainfall, and flooding. Not only dengue, another disease (eg. Water borne diseases) may follow (see section 3.4 for multi hazards response).

1.3.2 Community Awareness

Key points
  • Lack of awareness contributes to inadequate preventive behaviours, then leads to virus transmission.

Lack of awareness contributes to inadequate preventive behaviours, then leads to virus transmission. Low community awareness is associated with lack of knowledge about dengue. Communities may not be able to diagnose early symptoms of dengue. Limited awareness influences the community behaviour that increases the risk of dengue transmission, as follows: poor waste disposal, leaving uncovered water storage containers, discarded tyres, plastic containers and other water-holding materials provide ideal breeding habitats for Aedes mosquitoes. These challenges are common in dense populations with inadequate water, sanitation, and hygiene services. Moreover, the risk becomes higher among the vulnerable people, such as who are living in informal settlements, low-income communities, elderly, pregnant and lactating women, children, persons with disabilities and people living with chronic diseases.[1]

1.3.3 Population Mobility and Cross-Border Transmission

Key points
  • Population mobility such as unplanned rapid urbanisation and cross-border movement contributes to the continued spread of dengue across area even countries—as some countries in Asia Pacific…

Population mobility such as unplanned rapid urbanisation[1] and cross-border movement contributes to the continued spread of dengue across area even countries—as some countries in Asia Pacific lie on the same island with high cross-border mobility. This mobility complicates surveillance, early detection, outbreak control, and increases the need for coordinated preparedness and anticipatory action.

Chapter 2. Prevention, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action

Prevention is an effort aimed at reducing the impact of hazards and vulnerability[10] by trying to stop emergencies before they happen. By eliminating or reducing high-risk factors, organisations and communities can significantly minimise the impact of future crises. The prevention phase focuses on identifying hazards early and taking proactive steps to eliminate or reduce the likelihood of an incident occurring. This stage is centred on risk mitigation and long-term safety improvements.[11]

According to United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR), preparedness is the knowledge and capacities developed by governments, response and recovery organisations, communities and individuals to effectively anticipate, respond to and recover from the impacts of likely, imminent or current disasters. Preparedness includes such activities as contingency planning, the stockpiling of equipment and supplies, the arrangements for coordination, public information, and field exercises. A preparedness plan is needed to enable timely, effective and appropriate responses to specific potential hazardous events or emerging disaster situations that might threaten society or the environment.[12]

While anticipatory or forecast-based action is an effort to protect people before disaster strikes including outbreaks based on agreed early warnings or forecasts. It needs meaningful engagement with at-risk communities to ensure its effectiveness.[13]

2.1 Dengue Prevention and Control

Key points
  • Dengue is mostly found in tropical and sub-tropical climates worldwide, mostly in urban and semi-urban areas.
  • Community behaviours really play an important role to prevent the dengue outbreak, including water storage, plant-keeping and self-protection against mosquito bites.

Dengue is mostly found in tropical and sub-tropical climates worldwide, mostly in urban and semi-urban areas. However, recent cases show the increased prevalence in rural areas across some countries in Asia Pacific. Control relies mainly on surveillance and integrated vector interventions. Surveillance of infectious disease is defined as the systematic reporting, monitoring, and data analysis of cases.

Community behaviours really play an important role to prevent the dengue outbreak, including water storage, plant-keeping and self-protection against mosquito bites. Routine vector surveillance and control activities among community could improve resilience.[3-5, 7] Not limited to below preventive actions, National Societies could refer to IFRC Community Based-Health and First Aid (CBHFA) for implementing dengue prevention in more detail (see Annex 3.12).

2.1.1 Promoting Personal Protection

Key points
  • Wearing clothes that cover as much of body as possible
  • Using mosquito nets, ideally sprayed with insect repellent
  • Applying mosquito repellents to exposed skin or clothing (in accordance with product label instructions).

Preventive action could start from ommunity members to protect themselves first, particularly during the day and early evening. There are some preventive actions as personal responsibility as suggested by World Health Organisation (WHO)[1, 4] as following:

  • Wearing clothes that cover as much of body as possible
  • Using mosquito nets, ideally sprayed with insect repellent
  • Using window screens or closing window
  • Applying mosquito repellents to exposed skin or clothing (in accordance with product label instructions).
  • Using mosquito-control supplies, including mosquito coils and vaporisers
  • The distribution and promotion of Long-Lasting Insecticidal Nets (LLINs)
  • Indoor residual spraying
  • Outdoor space spraying of flying mosquitoes

The kinds of mentioned items could be contextualised based on local availability and public authorities' guidance. It is important to assess whether this is culturally accepted, accessible, and affordable in the context of intervention.

2.1.2 Health and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) Promotion

Key points
  • Health and WASH promotion are important components of dengue prevention because many actions to reduce dengue transmission take place at the household and community level.
  • Experiences from National Societies indicate that health and hygiene promotion, elimination of standing water, and destruction of mosquito breeding sites are commonly implemented as part of…
  • Health and WASH campaign or dissemination.

Health and WASH promotion are important components of dengue prevention because many actions to reduce dengue transmission take place at the household and community level. Community members can contribute to reducing mosquito breeding opportunities through appropriate water storage, management of containers and other potential breeding sites, and regular maintenance of the household and surrounding environment.[1]

Experiences from National Societies indicate that health and hygiene promotion, elimination of standing water, and destruction of mosquito breeding sites are commonly implemented as part of dengue prevention and vector control activities. Door-to-door visits and school-based activities have also been identified as the most effective approaches for raising awareness and encouraging preventive behaviours at household and community levels.

There are some good practices the National Society could adapt to raise community awareness on maintaining good health and WASH, as an effort to prevent dengue transmission. By working with partners and communities, these are some collaborative activities to deliver:

  • Health and WASH campaign or dissemination. This includes search and destroys campaigns, promoting safe water storage, and household water management (see section 2.1.3).
  • Reduce potential mosquito breeding sites. This may be delivered along with larvicide distribution, with dissemination on how to use it properly.

Promote behaviour change through regular community engagement. Health and WASH promotion should go beyond the distribution of information materials. National Society experience indicates that door-to-door engagement and school-level activities can be effective channels for raising awareness.

Social mobilisation for vaccination if part of the dengue control programme.

2.1.3 Vector Control

Key points
  • Currently, vector control is the only way to interrupt disease transmission.
  • Removing discarded containers that serve as mosquito breeding sites
  • Dispose of solid waste properly and remove artiﬁcial habitats that can hold water

Currently, vector control is the only way to interrupt disease transmission. Monitoring and planning control measures for dengue epidemics are crucial for preventing or minimising dengue outbreaks. Currently, there is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. Early detection and prediction of disease outbreaks are supposed to do for community surveillance systems.[14, 15]

Adapting from WHO guidance[1, 4, 5], there are some preventive actions through environmental sanitation to destroy mosquito breeding sites as follows:

  • Removing discarded containers that serve as mosquito breeding sites
  • Dispose of solid waste properly and remove artiﬁcial habitats that can hold water
  • Cover, empty and clean domestic water storage containers on a weekly basis
  • Apply appropriate insecticides to water storage outdoor containers
  • Remove standing water in flowerpots
  • Clean up used tyres
  • Avoid accumulating trash; garbage should remain in closed plastic bags.
Which interventions have NO evidence and are therefore NOT recommended?

Bednets are an effective way to prevent mosquito bites; but for dengue fever, these should be used as a preventive measure for those who sleep during the day or those admitted into hospitals. As the mosquito bites during the day, bednets during the night will not be an effective preventive measure for this disease.

Mosquito coils and aerosol bug sprays (containing insecticides) are not effective interventions to protect a person or household from the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. Research indicated that where mosquito coils and aerosol insecticides were used, dengue fever incidence increased. One explanation as to why this occurred was that householders using coils and aerosols relied solely on these anti-mosquito devices and did not adopt other more effective preventive measures. The cost for these items is another prohibitive factor for their use in widespread community programmes.

%Source: IFRC Epidemic Control Toolkit

Good Practice: Fiji’s Integrated Vector Control Strategy and LTDD Action Plan

Fiji experiences recurring flood-related risks that can increase the likelihood of outbreaks of leptospirosis, typhoid, dengue, and diarrhoeal diseases (LTDD). Recognising these interconnected risks, Fiji is developing a country-specific vector control strategy alongside an LTDD Action Plan to strengthen the prevention, preparedness and management of vector-borne and other flood-associated diseases.

Fiji is expected to become the first Pacific country with a dedicated vector control strategy, providing an opportunity to establish a more systematic and coordinated approach to vector control. By aligning vector control measures with broader LTD preparedness and action planning, Fiji can strengthen coordination among relevant stakeholders, promote risk-informed planning, and support earlier and more targeted interventions before, during and after floods.

This approach offers a potential good practice for other Pacific countries facing similar climate-related health risks. It highlights the value of developing context-specific strategies that connect vector control, disease surveillance, community engagement and disaster preparedness within a broader public health framework.

(Source: Interviews with Center for Disease Control (CDC) under Fiji's Ministry of Health and WHO officials in Fiji, 2026)

2.2 Dengue Preparedness

Key points
  • To optimise a dengue preparedness, the National Societies along with communities should know what risks they need to mitigate.

To optimise a dengue preparedness, the National Societies along with communities should know what risks they need to mitigate. It makes an effort to prevent disease transmission from becoming an outbreak. Risk mapping and identification of actions to reduce the risk are parts of community preparedness. The National Societies could refer to Red Cross and Red Crescent (RCRC) Movement’s Enhanced Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment (EVCA) guidance and toolkits (see Annex 3.1). This EVCA platform has been created to make the guidance, tools and other resources easily accessible to staff and volunteers.

PhaseKey activities
Pre-positioningPurchase and preposition of required materials and equipment.
Readiness phaseActivities focused on establishing coordination mechanism, risk mapping, capacity building, awareness raising.
Early action phaseActivities focused on elimination of mosquito breeding sites, vector control, risk communication.

Emergency preparedness phases (table from the draft, shown as text).

2.2.1 Preparedness on Seasonality and Environmental Patterns

Key points
  • Dengue transmission is influenced by environmental and climatic conditions, including seasonal rainfall and temperature patterns.
  • Preparedness should therefore include the development of a local seasonal dengue risk profile, based on available epidemiological, meteorological, environmental, and community-level…
  • Figure 1 shows the practical preparedness to understand the local seasonal pattern, monitor environmental and climatic conditions, use seasonal information to prepare before transmission…

Dengue transmission is influenced by environmental and climatic conditions, including seasonal rainfall and temperature patterns. Understanding the seasonal pattern of dengue transmission can help National Societies and their partners prepare resources, strengthen surveillance, and initiate preventive activities before the period of increased transmission.

Preparedness should therefore include the development of a local seasonal dengue risk profile, based on available epidemiological, meteorological, environmental, and community-level information. This profile should be reviewed regularly and updated when changes in climate, environment, population movement, or dengue transmission patterns are observed.

Figure 1 shows the practical preparedness to understand the local seasonal pattern, monitor environmental and climatic conditions, use seasonal information to prepare before transmission increases, and consider changes in environmental and geographical risk. A cases trend mapping across years is useful to forecast the peak season of outbreak within the country.

Water storage to check may include and not limited to:
  • Plastic drum or bucket
  • Flooded floor
  • Water tank
  • Flower tub and tray
  • Used discarded tire

2.2.2 Increasing Community Awareness

Key points
  • Community awareness is an important component of dengue prevention and preparedness.
  • Awareness of dengue activities should not be limited to the dissemination of information.
  • Use multiple communication channels, with prioritisation of schools as a community awareness channel.

Community awareness is an important component of dengue prevention and preparedness. Communities should have access to timely, understandable and locally relevant information that enables them to recognise dengue risks, adopt appropriate preventive practices, identify early symptoms, and know when and where to seek health care.

Awareness of dengue activities should not be limited to the dissemination of information. They should aim to support understanding and practical behaviour change, while providing opportunities for communities to raise concerns, identify barriers, and provide feedback.

Key points to include in increasing community awareness are as follows:

  • Provide timely and actionable information.
  • Use multiple communication channels, with prioritisation of schools as a community awareness channel. Children are good educators to their family members at their own home and neighbourhood.

To promote dengue preparedness within the communities, community mobilisation such as community-based surveillance (CBS) approach should be strengthened (refer to Annex 3.5). Community volunteers should be equipped to improve early detection of suspected dengue cases, community surveillance, health education and timely referral for treatment. National Society volunteers could refer to IFRC Epidemic Control for Volunteers (ECV) material (see Annex 3.11).

2.3 Anticipatory Action for Dengue

Key points
  • Anticipatory action or early action is an approach to prevent or mitigate potential hazard or disaster impacts before a shock occurs or potential impacts felt.
  • Intensify Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE--see Annex 3.7)
  • Strengthen community surveillance and reporting

Anticipatory action or early action is an approach to prevent or mitigate potential hazard or disaster impacts before a shock occurs or potential impacts felt. The actions implemented are based on agreed funding mechanisms that allow implementation once forecast thresholds or agreed triggers are met.[16] It also applied to disease outbreaks including dengue. However, there are no universal signals to recommend. Specific thresholds should be defined and validated according to the local epidemiological, climatic, and surveillance context. If the local or national dengue outbreak is declared by the government, it functions as a trigger that requires the National Society to do early action and response.

In early action, the activities will be focused on continuing eliminating mosquitoes breeding sites, vector control, and risk communication. Some practical activities could be conducted including:

  • Intensify community-based vector control
  • Consider targeted vector control measures
  • Intensify Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE--see Annex 3.7)
  • Strengthen community surveillance and reporting
  • Prioritise high risk and undeserved communities
  • Prepare and mobilise volunteers
  • Monitor the situation and adapt the action.
Example from Nepal (Simplified Early Action Protocol for Dengue (draft), 2026)

Trigger #1: Average rainfall and temperature

The Trigger will be reached when climate monitoring by the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM), using an agreed climate monitoring product, indicates temperature conditions associated with an increased risk of dengue transmission expanding into prioritised mid-hill districts above 1,500 metres elevation, corresponding to the identified climatic threshold of approximately 15.5°C.

  • Routine surveillance: when national mean temperature reaches 15.2°C
  • Enhanced Alert: when Temp 15.2–15.5°C Or P50 elevation rising
  • Emergency Response: when Temp > 15.5°C OR confirmed highland transmission

Trigger # 2: Dengue confirmed cases

The Early Action Trigger will be reached when EDCD surveillance data report 20 or more laboratory-confirmed dengue cases per week (or the equivalent monthly average of approximately 80 confirmed cases per month) in one or more prioritised mid-hill districts above 1,500 metres elevation, indicating sustained local transmission and increased risk of outbreak expansion.

The trigger thresholds were developed based on the preliminary climate and epidemiological analysis undertaken by the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre using dengue surveillance data (2019–2024). The Trigger#1 is based on climate monitoring by the government bodies of Hydrology and Meteorology using nationally recognised climate monitoring products and, where appropriate, gridded climate datasets. The Trigger#2 is based on the weekly dengue surveillance data that can be accessed through national published epidemiology data.

Example from Sri Lanka (Simplified Early Action Protocol for Dengue (draft), 2026)

The trigger for intervention is defined based on two scenarios: weekly epidemiological reports issued by the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU) and meteorological predictions.

Readiness Trigger: The Meteorological Department forecasts average rainfall exceeding 100mm in the Western Province. (There is typically a lag time of two to four weeks between heavy rainfall and subsequent dengue outbreaks.

Sri Lanka experiences two monsoon seasons, with the Southwest monsoon bringing the highest rainfall, particularly in the Western Province (Colombo, Kalutara, and Gampaha districts).

When average rainfall exceeds 100mm, it creates favourable conditions for dengue outbreaks in the Western Province, which can then spread to Jaffna and Kandy districts due to human movement.

Early Action Triggers: The trigger is activated under the following conditions:

  • Weekly caseload > 1,500 cases in the months of  May, June, July and December, and January

or

  • If the caseload in the target districts exceeds 1.5 times higher than their average caseload

This trigger point was established based on the average number of confirmed cases reported to the Ministry of Health (MoH) by the National Dengue Control Unit (NDCU) through the district-wise Weekly Epidemiological Reports (WER).

2.4 Cross-cutting Theme on Dengue Prevention, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action

2.4.1 Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI) in Dengue Preparedness, Prevention and Anticipatory Action

Key points
  • In assisting communities, National Societies should apply PGI principles (see Annex 3.9) within the dengue prevention activities, whether PGI focal point is available or not.
  • "Make PGI and RCCE as everyone's responsibility!"

In assisting communities, National Societies should apply PGI principles (see Annex 3.9) within the dengue prevention activities, whether PGI focal point is available or not. National Societies should prioritise vulnerable groups including children, elderly, pregnant and lactating women, persons with disabilities, people living with chronic diseases, and low-income households. This targeted approach ensures that early actions reach those most at risk and maximises the humanitarian impact of limited resources. PGI can be applied through equal opportunity to vulnerable or marginalised people. Community consultation, item distribution, and any other community activities should consider access to all members while applying to the local norms. For example, targeting males and females separately and being sensitive to their specific gender roles is essential when enlisting their support for vector control.[1]

"Make PGI and RCCE as everyone's responsibility!"

2.4.2 Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) in Dengue Prevention, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action

Key points
  • RCCE is how the National Society maintains accountability toward the communities (see Annex 3.7 for RCCE and Annex 3.8 for CEA guidance in more detail).
  • Using simple terms in local or national language, that can be understood by the community members
  • Appropriate illustration along with the information given, that is easier to help community members who are illiterate

RCCE is how the National Society maintains accountability toward the communities (see Annex 3.7 for RCCE and Annex 3.8 for CEA guidance in more detail). Community engagement efforts ensure that in delivering assistance, the National Society gives the community opportunity to participate actively. RCCE mainstreaming should be done although there is no RCCE focal person assigned in place. Below are some good practices in mainstreaming RCCE in dengue prevention, preparedness and anticipatory action.

Developing information, education and communication (IEC) materials to prevent disease outbreak. It may include health and hygiene promotion, personal and community protection, etc. IEC can be delivered in many forms, both electronically and physically. To reach the communities, IEC materials should be:

  • Using simple terms in local or national language, that can be understood by the community members
  • Appropriate illustration along with the information given, that is easier to help community members who are illiterate
  • IEC materials should be delivered according to the community preference, for example through door-to-door visits rather than mass gatherings. This preference should be consulted with the community (see point D: Community consultation).

Media engagement to raise awareness of the local population:

  • Mass media, such as radio, television, and newspapers
  • Optimise the utilisation of social media (photo, video, podcast, etc)

Establishing complaints and feedback mechanisms. This is appropriate to enhance accountability and improve service quality. Some good practices may include:

  • Community consultation about their preferences to share complaints and feedback (e.g. direct communication, message box, hotline call, etc)

Recording and Documenting complaints and feedback from the community. It helps the National Society to address any complains and feedbacks collected accordingly. A standard timeline to address problems should be set to improve community engagement and accountability during operations.

Community consultation. It is a vital part to enhance community engagement, that the community members are involved and actively participate to address their needs. The community consultation may include:

  • Planning community activities in preparedness and preventing dengue outbreaks.
  • Selecting targeted population, including defining the criteria of the targeted people during operations.
  • Consulting the appropriate schedule to distribute information (eg. IEC materials) to the community in times the community prefers (eg. weekend, afternoon to evening, holiday, etc).
  • Address misconceptions and risk perception

Awareness of dengue activities should respond to what communities understand, believe and do, rather than assuming that a lack of information is the only barrier to prevention.

Communicate risks about the disease or epidemic, not only to share information on prevention and mitigation measures, but also to encourage informed decision-making, positive behaviour change and maintenance of trust in the National Society response. This includes the identification of rumours and misinformation around disease.[1]

Activate Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) working group

RCCE working group may consist of National Society, relevant government institutions, academics, and other organisations.

This working group may have regular meetings to collaborate and manage risk communication among multi sectors in wider communities.

An example of selecting targeted area criteria
  1. Incidence of Dengue cases
  2. Mortality due to Dengue
  3. Gaps in services identified by the City Cooperation
  4. Lack of services from the government and other stakeholders.

7Adapted from: Bangladesh Dengue DREF Final Report, 2023

2.4.3 Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) in Dengue Prevention, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action

Key points
  • Illness leads to a reduction in productivity as people may not be able to work due to disease.
  • CVA can be used to address financial barriers faced by economically vulnerable households during dengue prevention, preparedness, and early action.
  • access appropriate mosquito protection and other locally relevant preventive items

Illness leads to a reduction in productivity as people may not be able to work due to disease. This can lead to a loss of income due to the reduction in work activity and to the diversion of resources to seek medical treatment.[1] The cash and voucher assistance (CVA) modality to financially support economically vulnerable people forms a critical part of any response operation and applies to the dengue response. This assistance can mitigate the impact of the disease on households that might otherwise be unable to afford preventive measures or medical treatment. By allocating funds to these groups, financial constraints do not prevent individuals from accessing necessary resources such as mosquito repellents and proper healthcare or even allow them (most vulnerable groups) the economic flexibility to remain at home, reducing the risk of further transmission.[17]

CVA can be used to address financial barriers faced by economically vulnerable households during dengue prevention, preparedness, and early action. Where appropriate and feasible, CVA can enable households to access essential goods and services, maintain basic needs during periods of increased dengue risk, and implement recommended preventive measures.

CVA should be considered based on needs, vulnerability, market conditions and the intended preventive or response objective, rather than being automatically provided to all households affected by dengue. Depending on the local context and the results of a needs and market assessment, CVA may support households to:

  • access appropriate mosquito protection and other locally relevant preventive items
  • meet essential household needs when illness or caregiving responsibilities affect household income;
  • access health services where financial barriers are identified
  • support transportation or other necessary costs associated with accessing health services, where appropriate
  • maintain essential household needs during periods when dengue-related illness affects the household's ability to work or generate income

CVA should complement, rather than replace, public health and vector-control interventions.

In the preparedness phase, the National Society should conduct data verification of the target communities. This step is required to ensure the targeted people are the most in need. The real challenges in the field include outdated data of community members. Early identification and verification may help the National Society to deliver CVA in a timely manner and to reach out the most in need.

During preparedness, the National Society should assess whether CVA is an appropriate modality for the anticipated dengue risk and establish the systems required for timely delivery. This should include:

  • identifying potentially vulnerable and at-risk communities
  • reviewing and verifying available population and vulnerability data
  • identifying appropriate targeting criteria
  • assessing market availability and functionality
  • identifying potential financial service providers and delivery mechanisms
  • establishing or reviewing beneficiary registration and verification processes
  • agreeing on coordination arrangements with relevant authorities and partners
  • preparing the operational procedures required for rapid activation of CVA.

2.5 Planning, Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting (PMER) in Dengue Prevention, Preparedness and Anticipatory Action

Key points
  • PMER is crucial in any operations, including dengue, whether PMER focal point is available or not.

PMER is crucial in any operations, including dengue, whether PMER focal point is available or not. Operations Manager should be responsible or assign one of their team members to carry out PMER works. According to the agreed prevention, preparedness, and anticipatory action, PMER should be delivered appropriately and timely to support the right decision making. Figure 5 below illustrates on how monitoring and evaluation are necessary to conduct, which is different for fast- and slow-onset.[18] This is adapted from the monitoring and evaluation in project/programme management cycle that is used to refer in long-term projects/programmes (Figure 4).

2.5.1 Planning

Key points
  • Need assessment: A need assessment is conducted to assess the community’s needs.
  • Developing monitoring and evaluation plan: It involves objective and indicators targeted, monitoring tools and documentation, monitoring and evaluation activities plan, and role…

Some activities to deliver in planning phase, including:

Need assessment: A need assessment is conducted to assess the community’s needs. Either independently by the National Society or jointly conducted with other humanitarian actors, need assessment is done by collecting information on epidemiological data, disease trends, and vulnerable populations.

Developing monitoring and evaluation plan: It involves objective and indicators targeted, monitoring tools and documentation, monitoring and evaluation activities plan, and role distribution within the team, including the communication flow from national, sub-national to community level. An example of monitoring and evaluation plan can be seen in Annex 2.

2.5.2 Monitoring and Documentation

Key points
  • Based on monitoring and evaluation plan developed, monitoring activities should be managed well, which means supported with evidence and well documented.
  • Monitoring should be supported by appropriate data collection tools, clear responsibilities, regular reporting, and proper documentation of evidence.

Based on monitoring and evaluation plan developed, monitoring activities should be managed well, which means supported with evidence and well documented. Monitoring should generate reliable evidence on whether planned activities are being implemented as intended, whether they are reaching the intended population, and whether adjustments are required.

Monitoring should be supported by appropriate data collection tools, clear responsibilities, regular reporting, and proper documentation of evidence. Information collected through monitoring should be reviewed and used to inform programme decisions, strengthen implementation, and capture lessons learned.

2.5.3 Suggested Indicators for Dengue Prevention, Preparedness and Early Action Monitoring

Key points
  • Below are suggested indicators referring to the Epidemic Control Toolkit for Response Manager (see Annex 3.14) that the National Societies can select which indicators aligned to their…

Below are suggested indicators referring to the Epidemic Control Toolkit for Response Manager (see Annex 3.14) that the National Societies can select which indicators aligned to their operations. The National Society could also use suggested indicators from the IFRC Indicator Bank as necessary (see Annex 2.2 and Annex 3.4).

Chapter 3. Dengue Outbreak Response

The National Society needs to assess the needs and their capacity to decide implementing outbreak response, as illustrated in Figure 6 below.

3.1 Dengue Case Management and Response

Key points
  • Dengue is mostly found in tropical and sub-tropical climates worldwide, mostly in urban and semi-urban areas. However, recent cases show the increased prevalence in rural areas across some…

Dengue is mostly found in tropical and sub-tropical climates worldwide, mostly in urban and semi-urban areas.[2] However, recent cases show the increased prevalence in rural areas across some countries in Asia Pacific. There is no specific treatment for dengue, however, the timely detection of cases, identifying any warning signs of severe dengue infection, and appropriate case management are key actions to lower case fatality rates to less than 1 per cent.[6]

3.1.1 Symptoms and Cases Monitoring

Key points
  • Real-time surveillance data could be provided by a well-documented case monitoring.
  • In some severe cases, dengue patients will need blood transfusions (Figure 8).

Most people who get dengue do not show symptoms. Individuals who are infected for the second time are at greater risk of severe dengue. For those who do, the most common symptoms[2, 5] to observe are:

Table 4. Symptoms of dengue (verify column mapping against your original table)

Mild dengueModerate dengue fever (warning signs)Severe dengue / DHF
Acute febrile illness of 2-7 days, plus two of: headache, retro-orbital pain, joint pains, myalgia, rash, arthralgia, body malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, flushed skin, swollen glandsPlus any of: high fever (up to 40°C), abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical signs of fluid accumulation, being very thirsty, mucosal bleeding, blood in vomit or stool, lethargy or restlessness, liver enlargement, rapid breathing, pale and cold skin; laboratory: rising Hct and/or falling platelet countPlus any of: severe plasma leakage including shock and respiratory distress, severe bleeding, severe organ impairment

Source: Adapted from Nepal Red Cross Society’s dengue cases monitoring

Real-time surveillance data could be provided by a well-documented case monitoring. It helps the National Society respond appropriately and practice data driven decisions, including assessing their capabilities, mobilising volunteers, and coordinating with relevant stakeholders. Below is an example from dengue case monitoring to health hospitalisation referral.[19]

In some severe cases, dengue patients will need blood transfusions (Figure 8). The National Societies should assess their capabilities to address this need.

3.1.2 Intense Preventive Actions and Community Awareness

Key points
  • Fogging.
  • Search and destroy.
  • Raising and maintaining community awareness.

In the response phase, preventive actions and community awareness should be continued intensively. Some additional activities could be considered to conduct:

  • Fogging. It can be provided when there is a case confirmed. However, it cannot destroy mosquito breeding sites completely. A regular household and environmental check remain crucial to reduce the mosquito breeding and disease outbreak.
  • Search and destroy. Community member could be mobilise to clean up their own household and environment to prevent the outbreak getting worse. The community leader or volunteers may encourage the community members to do it together.

Raising and maintaining community awareness. Health and WASH promotion should be intensively delivered to the communities. National Society may collaborate with local actors, leaders, or institutions to educate the communities to be more aware of the dengue risk and how to improve their healthy behaviour.

3.1.3 Community Mobilisation

Key points
  • National Society mobilise volunteers to provide long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), medicine, and testing kits to health facilities if necessary (according to National Society capacity…
  • Community volunteers are appropriately mobilised to monitor the case in their community and report it through a surveillance system or agreement with the local health services or government.
  • Adequate health safety measures to the staff and community volunteers should be taken, such as the use of mosquito repellent and mosquito nets.

The National Society should coordinate to activate community mobilisation from national, sub-national to community level. There are some key activities to conduct:

National Society mobilise volunteers to provide long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs), medicine, and testing kits to health facilities if necessary (according to National Society capacity and ability and referring to local or national protocol).

Community volunteers are appropriately mobilised to monitor the case in their community and report it through a surveillance system or agreement with the local health services or government.

Adequate health safety measures to the staff and community volunteers should be taken, such as the use of mosquito repellent and mosquito nets. In their daily activities to reach out to communities, National Society should consider in facilitating the volunteer’s transportation and safety procedures (for example, allowance and insurance) to deliver their responsibility, particularly to access the hard-to-reach areas.

3.1.4 Dengue Response Kit Distribution

Key points
  • Mosquito nets or bednets/long shirts.
  • Mosquito repellent.
  • Search and destroy toolkit.

The dengue outbreak may bring shock to some community members, especially the vulnerable or underrepresented groups, including the affected families. The kit should help families eliminate mosquito breeding sites, protect themselves from mosquito bites, and recognise when to seek medical care. According to local health instruction and community consultation, a response kit to distribute may cover item as follows but not limited to:

  • Mosquito nets or bednets/long shirts. It should be provided based on the community needs (including size and standard model) especially for the hospitalised patients and given with instruction of use.
  • Mosquito repellent. Following local health regulations, mosquito repellent may be included.
  • Search and destroy toolkit. It is useful to help families maintain their house clean from mosquitoes.

3.2 Cross-cutting Theme in Dengue Outbreak Response

3.2.1 Protection, Gender and Inclusion (PGI) in Dengue Outbreak Response

Key points
  • During a dengue outbreak, existing inequalities and barriers to accessing health information and services may become more pronounced.
  • During the initial and ongoing operation, the National Society should identify population groups that may experience different levels of exposure, vulnerability, or access to dengue-related…

During a dengue outbreak, existing inequalities and barriers to accessing health information and services may become more pronounced. The National Society should therefore integrate PGI considerations throughout the outbreak response to ensure that affected people can access information, assistance and health services safely, equitably and with dignity.

During the initial and ongoing operation, the National Society should identify population groups that may experience different levels of exposure, vulnerability, or access to dengue-related services. This should not assume that all members of a particular group have the same needs. The response should use available data and community feedback to understand which barriers exist and for whom.

3.2.2 Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) in Dengue Outbreak Response

Key points
  • collected through appropriate community channel

Before concluding the response, the National Society should provide opportunities for affected communities to provide feedback on the response and identify remaining needs or concerns. The community feedback collection may be conducted through:

  • post distribution monitoring (PDM)
  • survey
  • interview or focussed group discussion (FGD)

Each feedback should be:

  • collected through appropriate community channel
  • documented and analysed
  • addressed where action is possible
  • communicated back to communities.

3.2.3 Cash and Voucher Assistance (CVA) in Dengue Outbreak Response

Key points
  • CVA may be considered as part of the dengue outbreak response when affected households experience financial barriers that limit their ability to meet essential needs, access health services…
  • CVA should be based on a needs assessment and appropriate targeting, taking into account the socioeconomic impact of the outbreak, household vulnerability, market conditions and the…
  • prioritise for hospitalised patients and accompanying caregivers to cover food and immediate needs during hospital stay;

CVA may be considered as part of the dengue outbreak response when affected households experience financial barriers that limit their ability to meet essential needs, access health services or cope with the consequences of dengue-related illness.

CVA should be based on a needs assessment and appropriate targeting, taking into account the socioeconomic impact of the outbreak, household vulnerability, market conditions and the availability of other forms of assistance. It should complement public health, healthcare and community-based interventions rather than replace them.

Following the identification of an outbreak, the National Society should assess whether affected households are experiencing financial barriers that require CVA. The assessment may consider:

prioritise for hospitalised patients and accompanying caregivers to cover food and immediate needs during hospital stay;

loss or reduction of household income due to illness or caregiving responsibilities;

costs associated with accessing health services;

transportation or other essential costs related to seeking care;

ability to meet essential household needs during illness;

access to appropriate dengue prevention measures;

existing social protection or other assistance available to households; and

market availability and functionality.

3.3 Timely Outbreak Detection and Response: Applying the 7-1-7 Approach

Key points
  • The 7-1-7 target, developed by Resolve to Save Lives, provides a practical framework for strengthening the timeliness of outbreak detection, notification, and early response.
  • Strengthening early detection: Monitor epidemiological trends, unusual increases in reported dengue cases, and relevant environmental or climate signals to identify potential outbreaks…
  • Ensuring rapid notification: Establish clear reporting and escalation procedures, including designated focal points, communication channels and responsibilities for notifying the relevant…

The 7-1-7 target, developed by Resolve to Save Lives[20], provides a practical framework for strengthening the timeliness of outbreak detection, notification, and early response. It aims to detect a potential outbreak within 7 days, notify the relevant public health authorities within 1 day of detection, and complete initial response actions within 7 days.

For dengue operations, the approach can support timely information sharing and coordinated action among health authorities, National Societies, community volunteers, and other relevant partners. It can be applied by:

  • Strengthening early detection: Monitor epidemiological trends, unusual increases in reported dengue cases, and relevant environmental or climate signals to identify potential outbreaks promptly.
  • Ensuring rapid notification: Establish clear reporting and escalation procedures, including designated focal points, communication channels and responsibilities for notifying the relevant health authorities.
  • Facilitating timely early response: Maintain operational readiness, including trained personnel, supplies, coordination mechanisms and pre-agreed actions that can be initiated promptly when required.
  • Reviewing performance and learning: Document the time taken to detect, notify and initiate or complete early response actions. Where targets are not met, identify operational bottlenecks, responsible stakeholders, and practical measures to improve future performance.

The 7-1-7 approach should complement, rather than replace, the dengue-specific epidemiological and climate triggers defined in this guideline. These triggers determine when agreed anticipatory actions or other operational measures should be activated, while 7-1-7 helps assess whether detection, notification, and response processes are sufficiently timely and effective.

3.4 Planning, Monitoring, Evaluation and Reporting (PMER) in Dengue Outbreak Response

3.4.1 Monitoring and Documentation

Key points
  • During outbreak response, monitoring and documentation are required to be maintained.

During outbreak response, monitoring and documentation are required to be maintained. Monitoring should be used to track the planned activities that are being implemented well (for example, post distribution monitoring (PDM). Monitoring should always be supported with evidence to inform the operations decision making. The indicators to measure during outbreak response are referred to the suggested indicators as presented in section 2.5.3 (The suggestion from IFRC Indicator Bank can be seen in Annex 2.3 and Annex 3.4.)

3.4.2 Evaluation, Reporting, and Learning

Key points
  • The transition period should include a structured review of what work, what do not work, and what should be changed before the next dengue season or outbreak.

The transition period should include a structured review of what work, what do not work, and what should be changed before the next dengue season or outbreak. A learning process can be conducted through some activities, for example an after-action review (AAR), participatory group discussion with the community, early recovery assessment, etc. Evaluation and learning should be shared with the relevant stakeholders including community and incorporated into preparedness plans, early-action protocols and other relevant tools. The data collection specifically recommends sharing monitoring and evaluation results with communities, documenting lessons after a completed response, and promoting cross-country learning within the region.

3.5 Multi-hazards Response

Key points
  • Mosquito breeding and the dengue virus transmission are influenced by seasonal and environmental patterns.
  • Integrated Dengue Awareness Raising.
  • Dengue risk assessment and surveillance.

Mosquito breeding and the dengue virus transmission are influenced by seasonal and environmental patterns. It is the reason why dengue cases could also increase in the middle of multiple hazards or crises, such as dengue outbreaks during floods, cyclones, and other disease outbreak emergencies. During any emergency, dengue risk could be assessed too as part of public health risk comparison between before and after a hazard occurs. The response should be integrated, in coordination with local relevant authorities and actors.

Integrated Dengue Awareness Raising. Dengue awareness can be embedded in all emergency responses (typhoons, fires, evacuations). For example, dengue awareness raising is included during health and hygiene promotion — even during item distribution. The key messages should involve local conditions and promote early recognition of dengue symptoms and timely access to healthcare.

Dengue risk assessment and surveillance. Include dengue-related risks in rapid assessments and ongoing monitoring, considering local transmission patterns, environmental conditions, water and sanitation disruptions, population displacement, and potential mosquito breeding sites. Coordinate with local health authorities to monitor dengue trends and identify areas requiring additional preventive measures.

Prevention in evacuation centres and temporary shelters. Integrate dengue prevention into shelter management, WASH activities, and the provision of essential services. Promote safe water storage, adequate drainage, solid waste management, and the removal of standing water. Where appropriate, provide suitable mosquito protection measures based on assessed needs and local guidance.

Environmental management and vector control. Support communities in identifying and eliminating potential mosquito breeding sites in affected areas, including shelters, water collection points, and public facilities. Coordinate with relevant authorities to implement locally appropriate vector control measures in accordance with national guidelines.

Continuity of health services and referrals. Maintain access to dengue-related health information, surveillance, and referral services during emergencies. Ensure communities know where to seek care for suspected dengue and coordinate with health facilities to address disruptions that may delay diagnosis or treatment.

Coordination and community engagement. Work with local authorities, health and WASH partners, community leaders, volunteers, and other relevant actors to integrate dengue risk reduction into multi-hazard response plans. Engage affected communities in identifying risks, implementing preventive measures, and providing feedback on emerging needs.

The integration of dengue prevention should be proportionate to the assessed risk and adapted to the type and phase of the emergency. These activities should complement, rather than duplicate, existing health, WASH, shelter, and vector control interventions.

3.6 Transition to Regular Behaviour Change

Key points
  • The transition from outbreak response to recovery should begin when the immediate public health emergency has stabilised and the intensity of response activities can gradually be reduced.
  • The National Society, in coordination with relevant authorities and partners, should assess whether the situation has stabilised and determine which response activities can be reduced,…
  • the epidemiological situation and trends in dengue cases

The transition from outbreak response to recovery should begin when the immediate public health emergency has stabilised and the intensity of response activities can gradually be reduced. The transition should be planned and coordinated, rather than treated as the end of the response operation.

The National Society, in coordination with relevant authorities and partners, should assess whether the situation has stabilised and determine which response activities can be reduced, maintained, or integrated into routine programmes and services.

Before scaling down response activities, the National Society should review:

  • the epidemiological situation and trends in dengue cases
  • the status of ongoing surveillance and early-warning mechanisms
  • community needs and remaining vulnerabilities
  • the capacity of local health and community systems to continue relevant activities
  • the status of volunteer mobilisation and support
  • outstanding community feedback and concerns
  • resources and activities that need to be transferred to routine programmes or other responsible actors
  • the criteria for transition should be agreed with relevant health authorities and other partners and should consider the local context and national outbreak management protocols.

Chapter 4. Communication and Coordination

4.1 National Approach and Strategy

Key points
  • In dengue operations, the National Society is responsible to build and/or maintain communication and coordination with the relevant public authorities (eg.

In dengue operations, the National Society is responsible to build and/or maintain communication and coordination with the relevant public authorities (eg. Ministry of Health) and other actors at regional or national level, such as WHO, other humanitarian organisations, academic institutions, health services, etc. Dengue operations should engage in a multi-sectoral approach to create a wider impact.

Good Practice: One Plan Approach Dengue Response

Nepal Red Cross Society implemented a one-plan approach in times of dengue operations. All activities from prevention, preparedness, early action to outbreak response are delivered evenly in all districts across the country. There is shared funding allocation mechanism from several funding sources to cover the needs in all districts--consolidated under a single operational plan with shared indicators.

(Source: Interviews with Nepal Red Cross Society, 2026)

Good Practice: Cross-border Coordination

Indonesian Red Cross Society and Timor-Leste Red Cross has agreed and signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to coordinate and collaborate in times of hazards or disaster, including health emergency in cross border areas.

(Source: Interviews with Timor-Leste Red Cross and IFRC CCD Jakarta Office, 2026)

4.1.1 Stakeholder Coordination

Key points
  • National Society should initiate or get involved in national level communication and coordination networks with the relevant government and other actors.
  • Working with the RCRC movement, the operations team at national level could communicate and coordinate with IFRC or Participating National Societies (PNS) in-country/regional delegation to…

As an auxiliary of the public authorities, National Societies are responsible for working together with the government from national to local level. This effort will involve:

National Society should initiate or get involved in national level communication and coordination networks with the relevant government and other actors. It includes accessing the national data to decide which area to target in operation. Engagement with the national government also helps the National Society to respond appropriately, whether the government declares any scale of outbreak status that needs emergency response or only prevention required.

Working with the RCRC movement, the operations team at national level could communicate and coordinate with IFRC or Participating National Societies (PNS) in-country/regional delegation to access any technical or funding support (see Chapter 5).

4.1.2 National Society Development (NSD)

Key points
  • Internally, the National Society should prepare human resources and stockpiles.
  • Epidemiology: including dengue causes, virus transmission, and preventive action.
  • Referral system: referring to national or local referral system by the government or health services.

Internally, the National Society should prepare human resources and stockpiles. The operations team should take the lead under coordination and supervision of management leadership (refer to each National Society's structure and regulation). In preparing operations, the National Society should coordinate with its sub-national branch and its warehouse (if available) to manage the stockpiles.

During operations, capacity building for staff and community volunteers is necessary. This also contributes to enhance effective community-based surveillance (CBS) from community to national level, including real time surveillance and reporting (see Annex 3.5 for CBS guidance). Training materials to equip the staff and volunteers may include:

  • Epidemiology: including dengue causes, virus transmission, and preventive action.
  • Referral system: referring to national or local referral system by the government or health services.
  • Community engagement: how to communicate with the community members, including responding to rejection or complaints.
  • Accountability: including documenting and managing feedback from the community, monitoring, and reporting activities in the community.

Mainstreaming PGI: applying PGI principles in delivering information or conducting activities with the community, may include how to interact with community members without leaving behind the vulnerable people and implementing sex, age, and disability data disaggregation (SADDD) in data monitoring.

National Society development in dengue operations in detail can refer to IFRC Preparedness for Effective Response (PER) — see Annex 3.13.

4.2 Sub-national Coordination and Community Mobilisation

Key points
  • Coordination and community mobilisation at sub-national level should follow the national approach and strategy, to ensure the service quality and consistency to the communities.

Coordination and community mobilisation at sub-national level should follow the national approach and strategy, to ensure the service quality and consistency to the communities. This effort also contributes to strengthening Risk Communication and Community Engagement (RCCE) internally and externally through the RCCE working group (see section 2.4.2 and 3.2.2).

4.2.1 Community Volunteer Mobilisation

Key points
  • Volunteers’ mobilisation is the core operations mechanism of the RCRC movement.
  • Training or capacity building to community volunteers before mobilise them to the community.
  • Household/door-to-door visit.

Volunteers’ mobilisation is the core operations mechanism of the RCRC movement. There are some good practices suggested in volunteer’s mobilisation during dengue operations.

Training or capacity building to community volunteers before mobilise them to the community. The training materials may include dengue epidemiology, case monitoring, and how to communicate with community members as well as mainstreaming the cross-cutting themes (PGI and RCCE).

Household/door-to-door visit. According to National Societies staff and volunteers review, this method is considered effective to raise people’s awareness. However, it requires more time to allocate and volunteers to mobilise.

Distribution of IEC material (dengue epidemiology including symptoms, causes, and preventive action). Community volunteers are capacitated to deliver IEC materials contextually that are easily accessible and understandable by all community members, including the vulnerable or marginalised groups in an appropriate way.

Mainstreaming PGI and CEA while involved in monitoring and evaluation. In assisting the community, volunteers should apply the principles of PGI and CEA. Volunteers also have key roles in monitoring and evaluation as activity report and progress, that should be delivered to the National Society office or response team.

Activating the CBS mechanism within the community, in collaboration with the local authorities. It includes introducing a referral system to the community in coordination with the local health services.

Volunteers’ safety and security. With the responsibilities the volunteers carry, their safety and security in delivering services should be prioritised. Besides capacity building, the National Society should equip volunteers with support for example, allowance, insurance, or transportation support.

4.2.2 Local Actor Collaboration

Key points
  • Dengue prevention and response require collaboration with local actors who understand the community, local environment, and existing systems.

Dengue prevention and response require collaboration with local actors who understand the community, local environment, and existing systems. National Societies should establish and maintain coordination with relevant actors at the local level to support timely information sharing, community mobilisation, prevention activities and referral. Collaboration should not be limited to asking local actors to disseminate messages or mobilise communities. Local actors should also be able to bring information from the community back to the National Society and other response partners. The local actors may include local level government, religious leaders, schools, health services, and community groups.

Chapter 5. RCRC Movement Support

5.1 Technical Support

Key points
  • National Societies can engage with the IFRC country delegation, cluster or regional structures, and other relevant RCRC Movement partners to access technical support according to their…
  • Technical support may include assistance to analyse the dengue situation, assess risks and needs, develop or review preparedness and response plans, establish early-warning and early-action…
  • Dengue risk and epidemiological analysis, including interpretation of available surveillance and environmental information.

National Societies can engage with the IFRC country delegation, cluster or regional structures, and other relevant RCRC Movement partners to access technical support according to their needs and capacities.

Technical support may include assistance to analyse the dengue situation, assess risks and needs, develop or review preparedness and response plans, establish early-warning and early-action mechanisms, and strengthen monitoring and learning.

Depending on the context, National Societies may seek technical assistance in areas such as:

  • Dengue risk and epidemiological analysis, including interpretation of available surveillance and environmental information.
  • Preparedness and response planning, including development or review of dengue response plans and operational priorities.
  • Early warning and early action, including identification of appropriate indicators, triggers, and actions.
  • Community-based surveillance and risk communication, including RCCE approaches.
  • Vector control and community-level prevention, in coordination with relevant health authorities.
  • PGI and RCCE, to ensure that activities are inclusive, accessible, and responsive to community needs.
  • (Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning (MEL), including the development of monitoring frameworks, indicators, documentation and learning mechanisms.
  • Operational planning and resource mobilisation, where additional support is required.

National Societies should communicate their technical support needs as early as possible, particularly when dengue risk is increasing or an early-warning trigger has been reached. Early engagement can help ensure that technical advice is available before the situation escalates.

5.2 IFRC Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF)

Key points
  • Dengue response is aligned with the IFRC's regional epidemic preparedness and control priorities, focusing on supporting the Host National Society through training, awareness campaigns,…
  • The IFRC DREF is an efficient, fast, transparent, and localised way of getting funding directly to local humanitarian actors – both before and after crisis hits. On the left side is a…

Dengue response is aligned with the IFRC's regional epidemic preparedness and control priorities, focusing on supporting the Host National Society through training, awareness campaigns, distribution of educational materials, community-based surveillance, and communication of key dengue prevention messages in collaboration with the local authorities and stakeholders. Therefore, National Societies could access DREF to support dengue operations.

The IFRC DREF is an efficient, fast, transparent, and localised way of getting funding directly to local humanitarian actors – both before and after crisis hits.[21] On the left side is a summary of DREF application process the National Society should follow.[22]

5.3 RCRC Movement Collaboration

Key points
  • As a Movement, the Host National Society (HNS) and Participating National Societies (PNS) could collaborate in responding to hazards, including dengue.
  • Besides funding support, National Societies within the Movement could collaborate to respond in dengue.
  • Dengue transmission and population movement do not necessarily follow administrative or national borders.

As a Movement, the Host National Society (HNS) and Participating National Societies (PNS) could collaborate in responding to hazards, including dengue. One of the supports that can be accessed is contingency or flexible funds from PNSs to the National Society. The mechanism and qualification are varied, based on each other’s agreement. The form and scope of collaboration should be agreed between the relevant National Societies and aligned with the needs, capacities and priorities of the HNS.

Besides funding support, National Societies within the Movement could collaborate to respond in dengue. Since dengue is highly occurring in the region of Asia Pacific, coordination between neighbouring National Societies may improve each other’s efforts in preventing to respond dengue, particularly in cross border areas.

Dengue transmission and population movement do not necessarily follow administrative or national borders. In areas where communities, transport routes or population movements connect neighbouring countries, collaboration between National Societies can strengthen preparedness and response.

National Societies within the region can use existing Movement networks to share experiences before, during and after dengue operations. This can help National Societies learn from different approaches to prevention, preparedness, anticipatory action, outbreak response, PGI, RCCE, volunteer mobilisation and PMER.

Appendix. Data collection report

APR–AUG 2026  |  DENGUE OPERATIONS GUIDELINE DEVELOPMENT

1. Scope and Method

Desk review: 6 IFRC/international documents (IFRC 2023 dengue preparedness review; RCClimate 2016; WHO SEARO 2025 case management; WHO 2017 vector control; WHO 2024 RCCE toolkit; WHO 2025 dengue fact sheet) and 10 documents from National Societies (NS): Nepal (lessons learned, indicators, monitoring and communication records, MoH website, draft sEAP), Bangladesh (National Dengue Book, DREF report, critical analysis of national prevention) and Sri Lanka (DREF report, EAP).

Country mapping: 7 NS with dengue response experience identified via the Country Mapping Matrix (risk / NS capacity): Pakistan Med/Moderate; Afghanistan Low/Moderate; Philippines High/Moderate; Indonesia High/Strong; Timor-Leste High/Limited; Nepal High/Moderate; Bangladesh High/Strong. Six NS selected for in-depth assessment for representativeness across South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Pacific: Nepal, Bangladesh, Fiji (country visits); Philippines, Timor-Leste, Sri Lanka (remote). Fiji and Sri Lanka experience/capacity not yet identified.

Participation: 84 respondents through 11 FGDs and 27 KIIs, covering NS headquarters, branches, volunteers and partners (WHO, IEDCR, Ministry of Health, Danish RC, Swiss RC, IFRC). All six NS completed data collection; further regional information came from an FGD with the IFRC CD/CCD team.

2. Highlighted Findings

Preparedness and emergency response

  • Community-based surveillance and early detection
  • Vector control: larvicide, fogging, removing standing water and breeding sites, health/hygiene promotion
  • Door-to-door visits and school-based activities seen as most effective for awareness
  • Mosquito net distribution; clinical support and supplies (e.g. blood bank)
  • Case-based cash and voucher assistance (CVA), but distribution is not timely

Volunteers

  • Volunteer mobilisation is the core operational mechanism
  • HQ provides budget, protective equipment, training and minimal cash; travel, snacks and phone allowances only when resources allow (not guaranteed)

Partnerships

Other relevant actors: environmental and housing officials, police, military, village leaders, religious places.

3. Gaps and Challenges

4. Cross-Cutting Themes

5. Recommendations for the Guidelines

  • Early action: seasonal-calendar early warning and preventive action reflecting climate influences; multi-source surveillance triggers instead of reliance on politically sensitive outbreak declarations; clearer thresholds and institutional coordination
  • Community: make school-level awareness a priority channel for household behaviour change; engage youth, women and elderly groups
  • Systems: stronger NS–government information sharing; stronger MEL (share results with communities, post-response lessons learned); cross-country learning; contextual procurement standards
  • Context: cross-border dengue response; One Health and multi-hazard/multi-disease outbreaks; staff and volunteer safety regulations

6. Constraints, Challenges and Lessons Learned
